document.title: Comments of the Public Service Commission of West Virginia re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s filing to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service
document.group: PJM Large Load definition, Registry and Interim Resource Adequacy Service

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
COMMENTS OF THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION OF WEST VIRGINIA  
 
 
The Public Service Commission of West Virginia (“PSCWV”) respectfully files these 
comments to address concerns regarding PJM’s August 13, 2026, filing to establish Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) — a service to be implemented by PJM solely during 
periods when there are insufficient resources to reliably meet demand in real time operations. PJM 
explains that “IRAS will enable PJM to prioritize load reduction in zones/areas where New Large 
Loads have not brought their own new capacity or had their capacity needs covered through the 
Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”). New Large Loads can avoid this condition on taking 
transmission service by bringing new capacity to the system.” 
Thus, the only New Large Load (NLL) that will be at risk of prioritized or first-in-line 
curtailment under the new PJM proposal are those that have failed to cover their own capacity 
requirement (“Uncovered NLL”).1  Although the IRAS is targeted to Uncovered NLL, PJM 
attempts to navigate the maze between clear Federal jurisdiction over interstate transmission, 
implicit Federal jurisdiction over retail transactions that might affect wholesale electricity markets, 
and clear state jurisdiction over retail service and  rates.  PJM states that the IRAS “has been 
carefully designed to respect the cooperative federalism approach established under the FPA and 
animating several other recent landmark Commission determinations.”  PJM supports its filing to 
involve the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) in retail service describing 
                                                 
1 PJM refers to New Large Load that has not covered its own needs by supplying its own capacity as “Eligible New 
Large Load.”  That description is accurate and clear in reference to the IRAS, but we refer to that load more generally 
as being “Uncovered.”

2 
 
it as “an example of the federal regime helping to effectuate state decisions associated with the 
rates, terms, and conditions of retail service.” 
The PSCWV does not fully support PJM’s structure to address unusual and historic 
capacity needs created by growth in NLL, mostly associated with the growth of data centers, 
however, it does agree with the goals enumerated in the Administration’s Ratepayer Protection 
Pledge and similar ratepayer protections plans put forth by the Governors of the thirteen PJM 
States.  PJM refers to the Pledge and ratepayer protection in its filing and appears to understand 
the need to protect non-NLL customers (“Other Customers”) from costs associated with all NLL 
generally and  Uncovered NLL particularly.  Yet, its filing contains a provision to provide a 
wholesale rate credit to effectively pay Uncovered NLL for mandatory curtailments that are 
applicable to NLL only because they elected to add Uncovered Load.  It is that credit that the 
PSCWV opposes and requests that the Commission reject. 
The concept of compensation through any rate to be paid based on uncovered NLL that is 
interrupted is, if given to the Uncovered NLL,  the antithesis of everything that is intended to be 
achieved by the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.  PJM admits in its filing that: “A rate of zero dollars 
for IRAS would apply where Eligible New Large Loads “waive”2 in their retail rates receipt of 
compensation for the provision of wholesale Interim Resource Adequacy Service—an outcome 
that would be consistent with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge signatories’ commitment ‘to protect 
American consumers from price hikes due to data center energy and infrastructure requirements, 
and lower electricity costs for consumers in the long term.’”  Yet, by offering a rate, or 
                                                 
2 The PJM filing references the option of a lower or zero rate as residing with the Uncovered NLL to “waive” the 
Commission-approved rate credit, “agree” to a lower rate, or “voluntarily negotiate” to not receive the wholesale rate 
credit.  This is troubling since PJM later implies that who gets the credit is solely the choice of the retail rate regulator.  
Thus, PJM in its filling admits to the potential future tension between the pass-through of a rate credit federally targeted 
to a particular demand response customer to that customer or Other Customers.

3 
 
compensation, to Uncovered NLL for IRAS the PJM tariff establishes an unnecessary potential 
conflict at the retail level.  
If the Uncovered NLL receives the compensation, a cost is created that would fall on Other 
Customers.  Because that “cost” is solely due to payments to the Uncovered NLL, the PJM tariff, 
if approved, creates a cost that would not exist, but for the Uncovered NLL.  The only choice that 
States would have to prevent  rate increase on Other Customers is to prohibit the compensation 
from going to the Uncovered NLL and use it to offset the cost when setting rates for Other 
Customers.   
PJM defends its complicated and unnecessary payment to Uncovered NLL by assuming 
altruism of the Uncovered NLL.  PJM explains: “PJM’s proposal also allows Eligible New Large 
Loads to agree upon a retail rate between 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate and zero 
dollars, to further facilitate implementation of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and retail level 
arrangements.”  What happens if the Eligible New Large Load does not agree to a lower rate or 
zero?  If the Commission approves the PJM proposal it will set up a potential conflict if an Eligible 
New Large Load does not “agree” to waive its Commission-approved wholesale compensation for 
interpretability and a State retail regulatory authority denies it that compensation, which it would 
have to do to protect other Customers. This regulatory free-for-all could be further complicated in 
multi-state PJM Zones where the states have conflicting interests and policies for passing through 
the PJM IRAS compensation to Uncovered NLL or Other Ratepayers under their individual 
jurisdiction. 
The complexity, pitfalls, and potential for adding costs on Other Customers created by the 
PJM proposal can be simply resolved by rejecting the IRAS compensation.  It is unjust and 
unreasonable to pay Uncovered NLL for a capacity deficiency-driven curtailed when it could have

4 
 
been insulated from being first-in-line for curtailment by arranging for new capacity  but decided 
to go forward as Uncovered NLL, thereby creating the capacity deficiency.  
CONCLUSION 
The State of West Virginia, the other states in PJM and the White House have similar 
public policies that NLL, mostly data centers, must not come at the expense of residential or 
commercial utility customers. The PSCWV fully supports the West Virginia State policy that, 
consistent with the national Ratepayer Protection Pledge, developers will build, bring, or procure 
sufficient power resources and assume responsibility for infrastructure investments necessary to 
serve their projects. This approach reinforces the State’s commitment to ensuring that utility costs 
associated with large-scale data center development are not shifted to West Virginia ratepayers 
while promoting a stronger, more resilient electric grid.  While we believe there could be 
improvements to the PJM proposal to manage Uncovered NLL, it generally  furthers the goal of 
protecting Other Customers, except for the IRAS compensation to Uncovered NLL.  While West 
Virginia as a fully retail regulated state with vertically integrated electric utilities has regulatory 
tools to set retail rates for Uncovered NLL that protect Other Ratepayers, those tools could be 
challenged if the Commission approves the PJM wholesale compensation for interruption of 
Uncovered NLL and those loads do not “voluntarily” turn down receiving that compensation.  The 
PSCWV would have to order that the payments that were specifically calculated based on the 
Uncovered NLL not be assigned and paid to that load in order to protect Other Customers.  The 
federal/state tension that such action would set up is problematic, both administratively and legally.  
That tension is easily avoided if the Commission rejects that portion of the PJM tariff, which it 
should because the payments are not only unnecessary, they are unjust and unreasonable.

5 
 
Respectfully submitted this 3rd day of September, 2026. 
 
Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 
by counsel
